segments.say: A right-angled triangle. Watch the two short sides draw themselves: leg a is 3, leg b is 4, and they meet at the right angle - find the small square marker in the corner. The slanted side joining them is the hypotenuse, c, and we do not know it yet. Tell your partner: which side is c, and how can you tell at a glance?
questions: Which side is the hypotenuse, and how can you tell at a glance?
What does the small square in the corner tell you?

segments.say: Now a square grows on each short side. The square on a holds 3 by 3 - nine unit squares. The square on b holds 4 by 4 - sixteen unit squares. Keep both counts where you can see them: 9 and 16 are the numbers this whole theorem is built from.
questions: How many unit squares fill the square on each short side?
Where do the numbers 9 and 16 come from?
segments.watchFor: Students who add the lengths at this point and announce 7. Hold that thought visibly - and also listen for tan = adjacent / opposite. if tangent comes up early: the opposite and adjacent labels are exactly what that claim swaps.

segments.say: Now the square on the hypotenuse - the tilted square on c. Watch the nine blue unit squares and the sixteen orange ones fly in: every slot fills, none are left over, so the c-square holds 25. Open your student notes at the mechanism steps and check the count against them.
questions: How many unit squares fill the square on the hypotenuse?
What equation does the filled square give you for c?

segments.say: Here is the trap, and we are going to spring it on purpose. Adding the lengths gives 3 + 4 = 7, and the red bar of length 7 is visibly too long. The squares add instead: 9 + 16 = 25, so c is the square root of 25 - 5, the green bar. Read the trap section of your student notes, then check it against the worksheet example.
questions: Why is 7 too long to be the hypotenuse here?
What are the three steps, in order, for finding c?
segments.watchFor: tan = adjacent / opposite. Listen for the flip when students rehearse TOA quickly, and for c = 3 + 4 = 7 returning under pressure - send both back to the squares: 9 + 16 = 25.

segments.say: Work through the worksheet in pairs: square first, add the squares, then take the root - and for the tangent question, read TOA before you write anything. When you finish, swap with another pair and check their working against your student notes. Last, the exit ticket - on your own, no talking - and remember: if you can explain why c is 5 and not 7, you have cracked today's lesson.
questions: Talk me through the hypotenuse question: what did you square first?
How will you correct the flipped tangent claim on the exit ticket?
segments.watchFor: Pairs who write an answer before squaring. Require the two squares, 9 and 16 or their equivalents, to appear in the working before any total is accepted.
